**Mycorrhizae**
Symbiotic associations between fungi and plant roots, in which the fungus helps the plant absorb water and minerals such as phosphorus and receives sugars in return. In arbuscular mycorrhizae, the fungus sends branched structures called arbuscules into the root's cortical cells. All orchids depend on mycorrhizal fungi at some point in their life cycle.

**Hyphae and mycelium**
Most fungi grow as thread-like filaments called hyphae, which branch and weave together into a net-like feeding mass called a mycelium. Hyphae may be divided by cross walls called septa, or may lack them and be "coenocytic," with many nuclei sharing one continuous cytoplasm.

**Chitin cell walls**
Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, a tough nitrogen-containing polysaccharide also found in insect exoskeletons. This distinguishes fungi from plants, whose cell walls are made of cellulose.

**Yeasts, molds, and mushrooms**
The three most familiar kinds of fungi. Yeasts are unicellular fungi that ferment sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is why they are used in baking and brewing; molds such as bread mold are fuzzy filamentous fungi; and mushrooms are the spore-producing fruiting bodies of certain fungi.

**Beadle and Tatum and Neurospora crassa**
George Beadle and Edward Tatum used X-rays to create mutants of the bread mold Neurospora crassa that could not make certain nutrients. Their 1941 work supported the "one gene, one enzyme" hypothesis, that each gene directs the production of one enzyme.

**Saccharomyces cerevisiae**
Baker's or brewer's yeast, one of the most important model organisms in biology. In 1996 it became the first eukaryote to have its whole genome (16 chromosomes) sequenced. Its cells mate between "a" and "alpha" mating types using secreted a-factor and alpha-factor, while the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, used by Paul Nurse in Nobel-winning work on cell-cycle genes, divides by fission instead of budding.

**Lichens**
Lichens are symbiotic partnerships between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, either green algae or cyanobacteria. The photosynthetic partner provides food, while the fungus provides structure and protection, letting lichens act as pioneer species on bare rock.

**Ascomycota and asci**
Ascomycota, the sac fungi, is the largest fungal phylum and includes yeasts, Neurospora, and many molds. Its members produce sexual spores, typically eight, inside sac-like structures called asci, and many also reproduce asexually with spores called conidia.

**Basidia and clamp connections**
Basidiomycota, the club fungi, include mushrooms and puffballs and produce sexual spores on club-shaped structures called basidia. Their hyphae form clamp connections, small bridges across septa that help keep two distinct nuclei in each cell.

**Plasmogamy and dikaryon**
In fungal sexual reproduction, plasmogamy is the fusion of the cytoplasm of two cells without fusing their nuclei. This produces a dikaryotic stage in which each cell holds two separate nuclei, which fuse later in karyogamy.

**Penicillin and Penicillium**
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that the mold Penicillium had killed Staphylococcus bacteria on a culture plate, leading to penicillin, the first beta-lactam antibiotic. Other fungal products include the immunosuppressant cyclosporin, and Akira Endo developed the first statins from compounds found in fungi.

**Mycotoxins: alpha-amanitin, aflatoxin, and ergot**
Alpha-amanitin, made by Amanita mushrooms such as the death cap and the destroying angel, inhibits RNA polymerase II and is not destroyed by cooking. Aflatoxin, made by Aspergillus molds, damages DNA and causes liver cancer, and ergot fungi on grain produce toxic ergot alkaloids.

**Chytrids and chytridiomycosis**
Chytrids are mostly aquatic fungi with flagellated spores. One chytrid, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, causes chytridiomycosis, a skin disease behind the worldwide decline of amphibians and the extinction of about 90 frog species.

**Spitzenkörper**
An organelle cluster at the tip of a growing hypha that directs the delivery of new cell wall and membrane material. It organizes the tip growth that lets hyphae extend through their surroundings.

**Antifungal drugs and ergosterol**
Fungal cell membranes use ergosterol instead of cholesterol, so antifungal drugs such as polyenes (like amphotericin B) and azoles target it. Echinocandins work instead by blocking synthesis of the beta-1,3-glucans in the fungal cell wall, and these drugs treat infections such as Candida albicans (the cause of thrush) and Cryptococcus.
